findings.where: Hero, the first-person paragraph under Mark's line ('I advise multilateral development banks…'): four lines on desktop, eight on phone
findings.fault: Mark's own introduction is set as a long paragraph in widely spaced bold sans-serif capitals. That is a label style, not a reading style. It is slow to read, it sounds like a corporate banner shouting rather than a person speaking, and it breaks the tile's own type system, which says the sans is only for notes and labels. The next paragraph, the same kind of text in the same voice, is set in the serif body style. So the two opening paragraphs look like two different kinds of text.
findings.who_objects: Staff at development banks reading who Mark is: the one sentence that says what he does is the hardest text on the first screen to read, and it reads like a firm's banner. The founder would also object, because the brief's personal-advisor test needs Mark heard in the first person and rules out a look any consultancy could own.

findings.where: Hero action row: the email address between 'Write to me' and 'Book a consultation', compared with the same address in the footer
findings.fault: The same email address is set two ways. In the hero it is grey serif with a faint underline, squeezed between two sans-serif buttons. In the footer it is the blue sans-serif link style. In the hero row the serif address does not match the button labels on either side, so it looks like body text that strayed into the row of actions.
findings.who_objects: A visitor looking for how to reach Mark: the address the brief requires to be shown is the weakest-looking item in the action row, and it does not look like the same thing as the footer address.

findings.where: Hero margin notes (Istanbul 2025, Melbourne 2026, São Paulo 2024) on desktop
findings.fault: Talk titles of three or four lines are set right-aligned, so their left edge is ragged and each new line starts somewhere different. With a long title like 'Best Practices in PPP / Legislation for Emerging / Economies', the eye has to hunt for the start of every line.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who stops to read a note to see where Mark has worked: a short label can be right-aligned, but a several-line title set this way is harder to read than it needs to be.

findings.where: Hero heading, second line beginning with ‘perfect’
findings.fault: The opening quotation mark is not hung outside the text edge. At this display size it pushes 'perfect' in from the left edge the other three lines share, so the big line's left edge looks dented.
findings.who_objects: The founder judging the first screen first: the tile's one very large serif line is its showpiece, and a dented edge at this scale is the kind of finish a legal-journal look is judged on.

findings.where: Article specimen, the photo caption ('A radio interview at the Belt and Road Summit. Placeholder: …')
findings.fault: Two faces share one caption line: an italic serif caption and a sans-serif note right after it. The small text also has body-text line spacing, so the wrapped second line ('the image round.') sits far below the first and looks detached from it.
findings.who_objects: Angélique, who will publish captions with this template: the caption style is the pattern she will reuse, and as set it reads as two pieces of text with a gap, not one caption.

findings.where: Motion sketch timing table, the Start and Length columns on desktop
findings.fault: Values such as '120 ms', '900 ms' and '450 ms' break across two lines, with the number on one line and the unit on the next, even though the table has room to spare at 1440 px.
findings.who_objects: The founder reading the motion spec: a number split from its unit is slower to read and looks unfinished in a specimen meant to show care.
